fixes.explanation: Yes, "…fellow citizens with the saints…" Paul says they are "…no longer strangers and foreigners…" Strangers and foreigners got a new standing. They're citizens now, right alongside the saints.
Yes, "…members of God’s household…" That's a family word, baker, not a visitor word. Right before it, Paul says they are "…no longer strangers and foreigners…" Paul says they're in the household.
Paul says that at that time they were separate from Christ. That's the first thing on his list. Friend, I know a little about being left on the outside, but this is a whole other level.

Moses, the man God sent to bring Israel out of Egypt (Exodus 3:10), is a big name, so I get why he came to mind. But Paul doesn't name him here. He says the Gentiles were separate from Christ. Keep your eyes on that one name, baker.
Paul says the opposite. He says that at that time they were "…without hope and without God in the world." That's a hard line. The good news is coming right behind it, so hang in there with me.
That's right, baker. Paul says they were "…without hope and without God in the world." That's a heavy thing to read. Hold onto this one. You're about to see what comes next.
Right. Paul says Christ tore down the wall "…by abolishing in His flesh the law of commandments and decrees." He did it in His flesh. That's the line, friend, and it's a big one.

Travelers is a good-sounding word, but it isn't Paul's. He says they are "…no longer strangers and foreigners, but fellow citizens with the saints…" The word he lands on is citizens. So travelers doesn't fit the blank, baker.

Moses, the man God sent to bring Israel out of Egypt (Exodus 3:10), is a natural pick. But Paul says the building has "…Christ Jesus Himself as the cornerstone." That spot has a name on it, and it's Christ Jesus. Keep that one in mind, friend.
